newsitem.title: BURMA: Toned-down Burma New Year festivities end quietly.
newsitem.headline: Toned-down Burma New Year festivities end quietly.

text.p: Burma's traditionally raucous New Year's festivities wound down quietly on Wednesday as revellers faced heightened security due to government fears of possible unrest, residents said.
The four-day Maha Thingyan or Water Festival, when people douse each other with water and hold parties in the streets, is usually one time of year when Burmese can publicly gather in large groups.
But this year, warnings from the military government against unruly behaviour appeared to hit home.
"The Thingyan this year did not quite come off compared to previous years," said one resident on Wednesday, the last and traditionally most frenzied day of the celebrations.
Many said the quiet was due to increased security concerns and the obvious presence of more armed troops in the streets.

The government warns people against creating disturbances every year, but the warnings appeared more serious this year following recent religious unrest and a deadly bomb attack at a senior official's house one week before the festival.
The ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council, under its "Committee for Observing Discipline during Maha Thingyan", said it had posted officials around the city to ensure security.
A statement issued by the committee advised: "Stay clear of making disturbances and agitations that may lead to disintegration of national unity and a state of unrest".
Another warning threatened up to five years in prison for anyone caught making or selling water balloons or packets of ice and up to three years in jail for anyone caught throwing them.
Diplomats said before Thingyan began that there had been rumours of possible disturbances during the festival.
Authorities had feared a possible resurgence of the unrest between Moslems and Buddhists which rocked Burma in March, the diplomats said.
By Wednesday afternoon, there were no reports of any festival-related accidents or arrests on state-run media.
